author: Cunningham
note: Takht-i-Bahi monastery architecture; cites Xuanzang on two/three-storeyed pavilions of sangharamas

author: Cunningham
note: Takht-i-Bahi private houses; cites Xuanzang on plastered houses and windows

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: name of Raja Vara (Virat), given to the Takht-i-Bahi ruins, Yusufzai (Peshawar district), possibly connected with Po-lu-sha
evidence: local name Raja Vara/Vare for the Takht-i-Bahi ruins (older than the epic name Virat), heard from Hindu goldsmiths and Muhammadans
quote: I have brought the name ef Raja Vare thus prominently forward, because I believe that it may have some . connection with the famous Aornos of Alexander, and per
note: a name-connection only, not a site; in this volume (p. 42-43) Cunningham writes "Po-lu-sha, or Shahbaz-garhi" where the AG had Palodheri; Mizutani: Shahbaz Garhi

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sahri-Bahlol, Yusufzai (Peshawar district): the Dhamami stupa and monastery opened by Bellew; the high mountain = Takht-i-Bahi, 2.5 miles N
evidence: Sahri-Bahlol lies 2.5 miles S of Takht-i-Bahi; stupa and monastery excavated by Bellew; local name Dhamami taken from Skt. dharmatman "saint"; Cunningham dug ten statues out of the mound "Misri's field"
quote: I have already suggested that Sahri-Bahlot may be the city mentioned by Hwen-Thsang, where the Rishi Ekasringa had resided before the time of Asoka … In all these particulars Sabri-Bablel corresponds very closety with the description of Hwen-TPhsang. The high mountain I would identify with Takht-i-Bahi
note: Mizutani gives no site; Watters reports ASR V as "Takht-i-Bahai", but Takht-i-Bahi is the mountain and Sahri-Bahlol the site; the same passage writes "Po-lu-ska, or Shihbdz-garbi" (AG: Palodheri)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sahri-Bahlol: the great Dhamami stupa opened by Bellew (Peshawar district)
evidence: distances only: Faxian 7 days W of Taxila; Songyun 3 days to the Indus + 3 to Fo-sha-fu + 1
quote: which agrees exnotly with the position assigned to it by Sang-Yun … In this case E weuld identify it with the great stupa, called Dham&mi, which was opened by Dr. Bellew.
note: new = Xuanzang's stupa where the Bodhisattva "gave his eyes in a thousand lives" near Puskalavati (Gandhara; not in table); argued from Faxian and Songyun only; Xuanzang puts it at Charsadda, not here

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: ruins about Shahdheri (Rawalpindi district); hill Hatial/Athial above the city; head-gift monument in Babar-khana
evidence: second visit; new name Hatial/Athial for the hill above the city (added to Babar-khana, Seri-ka-Pind); pilgrims put the city three marches E of the Indus; ruins the most extensive between Indus and Jhelam
quote: In my previous account of the ruins at Shahdheri, I gave some very strong reasons for its identification with the ancient Taxila … This identification I proposed just nine years age, anda setond visit to the site, which I ave now sade, has only strengthened my conviction of its truth.
note: confirms the AG; also moves Songyun's tiger-feeding mountain (which Cunningham had put at Manikyala) to the hill of Sir-garh/Hatial at Taxila by reading "head" for "body"; Khairabad on the Indus = Songyun's fish-incarnation stupa (not in the Xiyu ji)

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: monument where Buddha offered his head
asr_identification: Babar Khana ("House of the Tiger") stupa and monastery at Taxila (Rawalpindi district)
evidence: two-storeyed monastery with square corner rooms (Xuanzang's corner pavilions), c. 60 monks; small railing pillar with a Kharosthi letter excavated at Seri-ka-Pind
quote: called Babar Khdna, ot “Ylouse of the Tiger,” I have suggested that it may have been the famous monument which Asoka érected on the spot where Buddha had made an offering of his head
note: repeats ASR II; Mizutani: Bhallar stupa, N end of the Taxila area (differs)

author: Cunningham
note: Manikyala tope measured after clearing; Xuanzang cited only in a footnote, no identification argued here

author: Cunningham
note: history: table-land between Indus and Jhelam tributary to Kashmir in 631 (Xuanzang); no location

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mallot (Malot), ancient city on the Salt Range, Jhelum district
evidence: route marched: Shahdheri to Mallot via Rawalpindi, Manikyala, Chakowal, Kalar Kahar 114 miles; via Fatehjang and Nila 101 miles, against the pilgrim's c. 117 miles
quote: The Chinese pilgrim Hwen-Thsang describes Seng-ho-pu-lo, or Singhapura, the capital of the Salt Range, as being about 700 Ui, or 117 miles to the south-east of Taxila … All these conditions are fulfilled in the site of the ancient city of Mallot … By this route the distance is just 101 miles
note: revises the AG, which put the capital at the Kotera fort above Ketas by reading 4-5 li for 40-50; Mizutani follows the AG (Kotera), so differs from Mizutani

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: stone stupa of Asoka with ten springs; stupa S of Singhapura
asr_identification: Ketas (Jhelum district), 9 miles E of Mallot: the Asoka stupa on the rocky spur (now a Bairagi's house) in the bend of the Ghata Nala, the deserted monastery 400 ft W; Singhapura's southern stupa to be sought N of Mallot
evidence: seven walled pools counted above the holy pool in a stream-bend 500 ft each side; spur 50 ft high; monastery 150 ft square with a well (being dug out for stone); pool names Vis-, Amar-, Chamar-, Kataksh-Kund; no occupation remains S of Mallot, ruins N of it
quote: I have already identified these springs with the holy fountain of Ketds', and as f have again visited the place en my way from Mallot … Ketis is exactly 9 miles distant from Mallot towards the east, instead of to the south-east … This identification is further confirmed by the existence of a ruined monastery on a mound 400 feet to the west
note: with the capital moved to Mallot the 40-50 li stand unemended (AG read 4-5 li from Kotera); Mizutani follows the AG for 03.04.03 and Majumdar (Kotera hill) for 03.04.02

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: place where the founder of the white-robed heretics (Svetambara Jains) attained his insight, with a deva temple
asr_identification: large ruined temple C at Ketas (Jhelum district)
evidence: basement 68.5 x 56.5 ft with dumpy pilasters and dentilled frieze, older than the Kashmiri-style temples above it
quote: fhe site of the Jaina temple may, I think, be sidentified with that of” the large ruined temple, marked C in my plan of the ruins of Ketfs
note: new = Singhapura: 白衣外道本師悟所求理初說法處 and the deva temple beside it (not in table); Cunningham reads the sectaries as Digambara and Svetambara Jains

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Harapa (Harappa), Montgomery district
evidence: Shorkot visited and found too small for 20 li; Harappa circuit c. 3 miles (Burnes); excavations (ground stripped by railway contractors): stone scrapers, pottery, and Major Clark's black stone seal with a humpless bull and six unknown characters
quote: But I have now visited Shorkot, and I have satisfied myself that it never could have reached the size of 20 li, or upwards of three miles in circuit, which the pilgrim assigns to Po-fa-to, wr Po-fa-to-lo. But- the size agrees almost exactly with that of Harap4,* and as the position otherwise corresponds, Y believe that Harap& must be the very city visited by the
note: revises the AG (Shorkot); agrees with Mizutani (Harappa). Rejects Julien's Parvata; Bavanni suggested for Po-fa but too small

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Asarur, large ruined city 60 miles W of Lahore (Gujranwala district)
evidence: Chach-nama: Jaisiya, son of Dahir, passed through Takiya on his way from Chitor to Kashmir; moulded bricks with dentils from Asarur
quote: Asarur is one of the large ruined cities of the Panjab, which I have identified! with 7'se-kaé or Taki, the capital of the country in the seventh century, when it was visited by the Chinese pilgrim Hwen-Thsang. In sup
note: confirms the AG (Asarur); Mizutani: capital perhaps new Sakala (Sialkot area) — differs

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Multan
evidence: name Mula-tana from a Kashmiri writer (Abu Rihan); sun-temple tradition traced through Biladuri, Abu Zaid, Masudi, Istakhri
quote: The earliest mention of Multin by name is that of the Chinese pilgrim Hwen-Thsang, who visited Meu-lo-san pu-lo or Mulasthdnipura in A. D. 641.
note: agrees with the AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Multan city and citadel
evidence: measured: fort 1.25 miles with 46 bastions; walled circuit of city and citadel 15,000 ft (nearly 3 miles), with suburbs 4.5-5 miles = 30 li; walls dismantled by Cunningham in 1854
quote: Altogether +the walled circvit of Multan, including beth city and citadel, is 15,000 fept, or very nearly three miles; and the whole circuit of the place, including the unwalied suburbs, is from four and half te five miles. This fast measurement ae exactly with the estimate of Hwen-Thsang, who makes the circuit of Muttin 30 #, or just five miles.
note: same figures as the AG

author: Cunningham
note: genealogy: U-ti-to (Udita) of Jalandhara = Adima of the Katoch lists; chronology only

author: Cunningham
note: genealogy: Atr Chand of the Baijnath inscription = Udita of Jalandhara; chronology only

author: Carlleyle
note: Bais tribe and Harsha; tribal speculation

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: Gridharakonta; Buddha's meditation cave and Ananda's cave
asr_identification: caves on the spur at the NE side of the northern range inside old Rajgir (Patna district), reached by skirting the range NE from the north entrance; not the Son Bhandar
evidence: second visit to Rajgir with extracts of Xuanzang from Cunningham
quote: I followed the first route, and naturally enough identified the Son Bhandar and the broken cave with Buddha’s meditation caveand Ananda’s . cave: but the extracts from Hwen Thsang shew that I ought to have followed the second route; this I have now done, and am compelled to consider my previous identifications of these two caves incorrect.
note: prefatory Note revising Beglar's own report (pp. 89-99, passages 263-272); his objections to Cunningham's Son Bhandar = Saptaparni cave are left "assailable"

author: Beglar
asr_identification: cave with two openings at the foot of the rocky peak on the Sailagiri spur; Ananda's place = cave 50 ft NW with sculptures or the great block 100 ft NW
evidence: two caves, one with Gupta-period sculptures and a head of Buddha; levelled terrace on the peak with brick buildings and a small tope c. 8 ft in diameter
quote: There cannot be a doubt, I think, that here is the cave mentioned by Ilwen Thsang and Fa Hian as Buddha’s meditation cave … but the great stone is, perhaps, the real spot, although it is not a cave
note: consistent with the AG's Sailagiri for Grdhrakuta, where Cunningham found no cave

author: Beglar
asr_identification: in the "northern shade" of the craggy ridge on the Sailagiri spur, Rajgir
evidence: traced the ramp/wall R.R. and judged it a line of defence, not the road to the caves; natural ascent from Q at the SE foot of the spur
quote: t.e cave which I consider Buddha’s meditation cave is accordingly situated in the “northern shade’’ of this craggy ridge. From Hwen Thsang’s detaiied account it does not appear to me that the sloping ramp or wall R.R. was meant as a road to these caves

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: stone on which Buddha walked; rock where he dried his clothes
asr_identification: long ledge of rock and a flattish rock in the torrent bed near the caves on the Sailagiri spur; main peak of Sailagiri crowned by a brick ruin
evidence: brick well of Xuanzang not found, only a rock cistern; brick ruin on the summit 20 x 15 ft, too narrow for a tope
quote: Near these is a long ledge of rock which I take to be the long stone mentioned by Ilwen Thsang over which Buddha used to walk. Close to, and almost in the very bed of, the torrent is a huge flattish rock in a sloping position, which I take to be the rock on which he dried his clothes.

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Patna
quote: This great city was anciently known by the name of Pdtaliputrapura, or Pushpapura or Kusumapura, and although from Hwen Thsang it would appear that Pdtali
note: notes that Xuanzang keeps Pataliputra and Kusumapura distinct; no new evidence here

author: Beglar
note: route of the Pandavas Mithila-Rajagriha inferred from Xuanzang's route Vaisali-Mithila-Nepal-Vaisali-Patna; no place located

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: stupa over the measuring vessel (Drona stupa)
asr_identification: small brick stupa at Bhagwanganj near Bhartpura on the Punpun (Patna district), 17 miles SE of the asylum stupa at Arrah
evidence: bearing and distance from Arrah followed on the ground; stupa 35-40 ft diameter, c. 20 ft high, bricks 12 x 14 in. in mud, square socket-hole 18 in. at the top; small temple mounds around
quote: Taking measurements and bearings from Arrah as the site of the asylum stipa, the site of the Drona stdpa falls somewhere in the vicinity of Bhartpura … my labours were soon rewarded by the discovery of a small stipa at BhagwAnganj
note: differs from the AG (vessel stupa at Deghwara near Chapra; asylum stupa at Chapra) — Cunningham had since moved the asylum stupa to Arrah; Mizutani gives no site for 07.02.04 and keeps 07.02.03b near Chapra

author: Beglar
asr_identification: from the Bhagwanganj stupa NE across the Ganges, 140-150 li from the Ganges to Vaisali
evidence: Cunningham's literal rendering of the passage; stone-and-brick temple 40 ft square 2 miles from Bhagwanganj and a temple mound 45 ft square near Bihta on the Punpun
quote: Clearly the 140 or 150 i refers to the distance of Vaisali from the Ganges; and so the accordance with my views is perfect.
note: rejects the AG's suggestion that "Ganges" is a mistake for the Gandak

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: stupa over the measuring vessel, on the bank of a river
asr_identification: Drona stupa near the old course of the Son, which then joined the Ganges at Fatuha
evidence: river course: the Son flowed to Fatuha until the Buddha's time; Xuanzang's silence on a river crossing between Arrah and the stupa left undecided
quote: In A. D. 630 to 640, when Hwen Thsang visited India, he went to the stapa built over the measuring vessel, which was on the banks of a river.
note: river-course argument for 07.02.04

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: small rocky hill SW of the old palace (Upagupta); five stupas; Kukkutarama
asr_identification: Bhika Pahari (Panj Pahari), small rocky hill 1 kos SW of Patna bazar; five stupas at its foot; Kukkutarama = small brick mound SE of Patna
evidence: local names Bhika Pahari ("hill of the Bhikhus") and Panj Pahari (where Akbar surveyed the fort); no relics of Pataliputra in modern Patna, so the old city taken to be under the Ganges
quote: The name of the hill Bhik4 Pahtri, meaning the hill of the Bhikhus (or mendicant monks), is so clear a record of its ancient purpose, that further comment is needless … To the south-east of Paina -there is yet a small brick mound ; its name has escaped me, but it is clearly the ruins of Asoka’s Kukkutarimé monastery
note: new = XZ's small stone hill with rock-dwellings for Upagupta and the five stupas SW of it (not in table); Cunningham (ASR XI, passages 323-324) puts the five stupas at the Panch-Pahari mounds and finds no Kukkutarama; Mizutani: no site for 08.03.01

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Tillara (Telara), between the Sona and Katar branches of the Phalgu (Patna district)
evidence: inscription on the door jamb of the Sangin Masjid naming Teladaka (read by Cunningham); high mound at NW end, half-mile of building undulations; 25-28 miles due S of Patna
quote: An inscription cut on the jamb of the doorway to the present Sangin Masjid at Tilldra distinctly mentions the name Telidaka. On submitting the inscription to General Cunningham, he at once read the name as Tel
note: confirms the AG (Tillara) with epigraphic proof; agrees with Mizutani

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: mountain from which Buddha contemplated Magadha; Gunamati monastery
asr_identification: Barabar hills (peak Surajink with an old temple of Siddheswara), Gaya district; Gunamati = Dharawat, ruins at the pass in Ratani hill
evidence: Xuanzang's bearings and distances followed without correction; old temple basement on Surajink; brick mounds and terraces along the Ratani pass with statues dug out by villagers
quote: This mountain General Cunningham, applying his proposed corrections, sceks in the range which runs from Gaya to Girak. But in this part of the pilgrim’s route I think no correction is needed. Adopting his bearing and distance, the spot falls in the group of isolated hills now known as the Barabar hills … Adopting his bearing and distance, we get to the village of Dharawat.
note: differs from the AG (range between Giryek and Gaya near Vazirganj; Gunamati near Nidawat); agrees with Mizutani for 08.04.02 (Barabar); Mizutani has no site for Gunamati; Cunningham adopts both in ASR XI (passage 324)

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Gunamati = Dharawat; Silabhadra = Kauwa-dol isolated hill, Gaya district
evidence: 20 li SW followed on the ground; at the SE foot of Kauwa-dol a large stone temple with granite pillars and a colossal seated Buddha, one pedestal with the Buddhist creed in Kutila letters
quote: General Cunningham has described Dharéwat, but it is strange that while describing it, the close coincidence between the remains here and Hwen Thsang’s account of the Gunamati monastery did not strike him … Following the pilgrim’s bearing and distance, we get to the vicinity of the isolated Kauwa-dol hill.
note: differs from the AG (Silabhadra at Bithawa hill); Mizutani gives no site

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Kauwa-dol temple; Gaya 12 miles SW by the old road along the E bank of the Nairanjana
evidence: distance 12 miles and bearing SW; the Nairanjana crossing explained by a return to the old Teladaka-Gaya road
quote: From the Silabhadra monastery, which I identify with the Kauwa-dol temple, Hwen Thsang went 40 or 50 Ji south … ‘lhe actual distance of the north end of Gaya from here is 12 miles; the bearing is about south-west.

author: Beglar
note: old roads Gaya-Telada-Patna; Xuanzang cited only for having used the Patna-Telada road

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Dulmi (Manbhum district)
quote: through or close to Dulmi (which I shall subsequently show to be Hwen Thsang’s Kirana Suvarna)
note: announced only; the argument (passage 273) settles on Sapharan opposite Dulmi; differs from the AG (Bara Bazar, Barabhum) and Mizutani (Rangamati, Murshidabad)

author: Beglar
note: Bodh Gaya temple pinnacle and date; Xuanzang cited for its Brahman builder

author: Beglar
note: Bodh Gaya temple date (against Fergusson); Xuanzang cited for its Brahman builder

author: Beglar
note: Bodh Gaya temple: Sasanka story used to explain the walled-up sanctum

author: Beglar
note: Bodh Gaya temple: upper chamber added later, as Xuanzang says; architecture

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Giriyak hill: the Giddha-dwar cave facing S at the top of the pass between the two converging ranges (Patna district)
evidence: Shekbir cave at the N foot said to communicate with Giddha-dwar
quote: I think there cannot be a doubt that the cave referred to is the Giddha-dwdr cave which faces south, and is at the top, not of the mountain, but of the pass
note: agrees with the AG and Mizutani; sides with Cunningham against Broadley that Faxian's hill is the same

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: stupa near a small isolated hill by Yashtivana; great cave of the Asuras
asr_identification: small tumulus beside a small detached hill near Sonagiri, in the defile between the Baibhar and Sona hills W of old Rajgir (seen from Baibhargiri only); natural cave on Baibhargiri too far E for the Asura cave
evidence: stupa-like mound seen with binoculars from the top of Baibhar; valley jungle impenetrable; vapour over the Tapoban hot springs
quote: close to this I could see a small tumulus having precisely the appearance of an old stipa. The position corresponds accurately with Hwen Thsang’s description, and I have no doubt in my own mind that it is the long and vainly-looked for stapa … but from its position it appears too far east to coincide with Hwen Thsang’s Asur’s cave
note: not verified on the ground; Mizutani: 09.02.03b recess of Pansabda SW of Handia hill, 09.02.03c unidentified

author: Beglar
asr_identification: list of seven caves; Asura cave near Yashtivana not yet found; Pippal cave and Devadatta's cave (Cunningham) accepted
quote: The Asur’s cave or palace of the Asuras, mentioned by Hwen Thsang as somewhere near Yashti Vana; it has not yel been found … As I differ in toto from General Cunningham’s identifi
note: rejects Cunningham's Son Bhandar = Saptaparni cave (AG, ASR I, III)

author: Beglar
asr_identification: cave on the slope of Vipula marked M ("Devadatta's house") on Cunningham's plan, ASR III pl. 41
evidence: cave found by Cunningham but omitted from his text; Beglar used Cunningham's manuscript map
quote: This cave is situated on the slope of Vipula, and is indeed marked in plate 41, 38rd volume reports, with the letter M … This cave, therefore, may be appropriately called Devadatta’s cave.
note: Mizutani gives no site (only = Faxian's cave)

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Sattapanni = large natural cavern facing W on the N slope of Baibhar, less than a mile W of the Pippal cave; the Son Bhandar and its neighbour = Buddha's and Ananda's caves
evidence: walked Faxian's route W from the Pippal cave and found the cave, invisible from the E; the Son Bhandar faces S and gets the sun, so not in the "northern shade"
quote: Going 5 or 6 & or about a mile west from here, in the northern shade of the hill is the famed Sattapanni cave … it is situated rather less than a mile from the Pippal cave, and to west of it
note: differs from the AG (Son Bhandar on the S face of Baibhar); Mizutani only "on Baibhara hill"; the Son Bhandar = Buddha's cave is withdrawn in his prefatory Note (passage 241)

author: Beglar
asr_identification: N side of Baibhar hill, in the bamboo forest
quote: Au Nord d une Montagne Situe au midi au Melieu d’une vaste bois de bambous il y a une grande Maison en pierre
note: quotes Xuanzang second-hand from Broadley (JASB 1872) with Ceylonese and Burmese accounts

author: Beglar
asr_identification: N slope of Baibhar hill (the "northern shade")
evidence: names Webhara and Cheti derived from Baibhar and its peak Chhata
quote: I have already combated Genera] Cunningham’s ingenious attempt to make out this expression as meaning that the cave faced the south … The cave I now propose as the Saptaparnna cave fulfils this condition.
note: against Cunningham's reading of "northern shade"

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: Saptaparnna cave; tope W of it
asr_identification: cavern on the N slope of Baibhar with brick-stepped approach, half-way platform and a chaitya just W
evidence: two brick-stepped paths converging on a platform; ruined chaitya W of the cave where Xuanzang puts a tope; natural boulder = pulpit; room for 500
quote: General Cunningham tells me that Hwen Thsang states distinctly the existence of a tope situated to westward of the cave and close to it. The position of the chaitya, which I here notice, occupies the previse position required by Hwen Thsang’s account

author: Beglar
name_in_asr: Saptaparnna cave in the bamboo forest
asr_identification: N slope of Baibhar, outside the old city
quote: The Barmese account implies that the cave selected was in the bamboo forest; Hwen Thsang’s account does the same. The cave I have suggested is in the bamboo forest

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Daryapur Parvati (Garh Paravat hill on the Sakri), Monghyr/Patna border
evidence: 13 large and 5-6 small mounds on the SE spur; brick tope 15-18 ft on the N peak dug to the rock, nothing found (coral beads and coins earlier)
quote: General Cunningham has suggested that this may be the site of Hwen-Thsang’s Parvata, or pigeon monastery

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Parvati hill, Daryapur Parvati
evidence: pigeons nesting in the hill's crevices; name Paravata; numerous Buddhist structures; bearing and distance from Giriyak do not agree
quote: I think We may safely regard it as the site of Hwen Thsang’s pigeon Monastery, although its bearing and distance from Giriyak 0 not agree with his account.
note: differs from the AG and Mizutani (Bihar, emending 150-160 li to 50-60); Cunningham in ASR XI (passages 329-330) prefers Soh-sarai N of Bihar

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Son Bhandar is not the Sattapanni cave (but Faxian's cave of Buddha's meditation)
quote: I submit that, although there is no doubt Buddha used to meditate in the Son-Bhandar cave, it by no means follows that the cave as we see itis the same as Buddha used it.
note: rejects the AG's Son Bhandar = Saptaparni; the Son Bhandar = Buddha's cave view is itself withdrawn in the prefatory Note (passage 241)

author: Beglar
asr_identification: Sapharan near Suisa, opposite Dulmi (Manbhum district)
evidence: numerous remains here (Jain figures, statues) against few at Bara Bazar; place-name Sapharan; Karanpur subdivision of Chutia Nagpur whose rajas traditionally ruled Dulmi
quote: In his geography, General Cunningham, following the ‘bearings and distances of Hwen-Thsang, places his Kirana Sufalana near Bard Bazar. As there are not many ruins there, while here the remains are numerous … Kirana Sufalana may with much probability be identified with the SApharan near this place
note: revises the AG (Bara Bazar, Barabhum); differs from Mizutani (Rangamati, Murshidabad district)

author: Cunningham
note: Gupta era: Dhruvabhata of Valabhi as king at Xuanzang's visit; chronology

author: Cunningham
note: Gupta era and Dhruvabhata; chronology

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Chi-ki-to = Chedi (Chedi-desa of the Kalachuris, upper Narbada); Maheswarapura = Seronj, NE of Bhilsa
evidence: Chinese syllables re-read as Chi-ke-da (cf. Ptolemy's Sageda); Ujain to Besnagar/Sanchi 142 miles by perambulator; bearings of the Travels and the Life compared
quote: whole name may, therefore, be transcribed as Ohuke-da ; and in this form it ojQSsra suc^ a s^ooarkable similarify to the … Seronj, to the north-east of Bhilsa, would suit these conditions almost exactly. And from, thence to Chedi the distance corresponds very well with 1,000 1% or 167 miles; but the bearing is south-east.
note: revises the AG (Jajhoti/Khajuraho; Maheswarapura = Mandla); differs from Mizutani (undecided: Bundelkhand or Chitor; Gwalior); Hall first suggested Chikito = Chedi

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Thakkiya district of the Rajatarangini = Takiya of the Chach-nama (Panjab)
evidence: Rajatarangini and Chach-nama name the district
quote: Tbakkiya mast be the district called Twe-hia or Tiakia by Hwen^Thsang, and the T&kiya which was visited by Jaisiya
note: footnote

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Thakkiya, close to Sangala in the Panjab
evidence: Rajatarangini: Bhoja of Kanauj overran Thakkiya c. 883-901
quote: Thakkiya is no doubt the same district as the Tdki of Hwen Thsang, close to Sangala in the Panj&b
note: Sangala = AG's Sanglawala-Tiba; Mizutani: Sialkot

author: Cunningham
note: Sasanka of Karnasuvarna and Gauda; history

author: Cunningham
